title: Aang’s Terrible, Wonderful Idea
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 24 of 40
content:
Aang’s terrible idea began with the sentence, “Technically, I checked the rules.”

I put down my tea.

Katara closed her eyes.

Toph grinned.

“No,” Katara said.

“You don’t know what it is.”

“I know you.”

“That’s unfair.”

“Is it?”

Aang stood in our kitchen wearing the expression he had whenever being the Avatar temporarily became less important than being the same person who once invented an air scooter because walking was boring.

He held four paper tickets.

Toph tilted her head. “Race?”

Aang looked betrayed. “How did you know?”

“You’re vibrating.”

“I am not.”

“You are emotionally vibrating.”

I took one ticket from his hand.

WINTER FOUNDERS’ FESTIVAL — CHARITY STREET COURSE.

Below it, in smaller print:

NON-MOTORIZED VEHICLES ONLY. BENDING-PROPULSION PERMITTED IN OPEN CLASS.

I looked at Aang.

“No.”

His face fell.

“I haven’t explained.”

“You want us to enter.”

“Yes.”

“In what vehicle?”

His grin returned.

That was the second warning.

The vehicle was in the courtyard.

Calling it a vehicle was generous.

It looked like a tea cart had fallen in love with a glider and produced offspring during a storm.

Four wheels. Wooden frame. Cloth wing. Steering bar. Two seats in front, two in back. A metal plate ran beneath the chassis for Toph to bend against if necessary. A small water reservoir sat behind Katara’s seat.

I stared.

Katara stared.

Toph walked around it once, feeling the metal through her feet.

“This is the stupidest thing you’ve ever built.”

Aang beamed. “Thank you.”

“I wasn’t complimenting you.”

“I’m keeping it.”

I circled the machine.

“Who designed the brakes?”

Aang pointed at Sokka’s signature scratched into the rear axle.

I relaxed slightly.

Then I noticed a second note underneath.

TOPH CHANGED THEM. GOOD LUCK.

I stopped relaxing.

The race was two days later.

We spent those days arguing about roles.

Aang wanted to steer.

Katara said Aang’s idea of steering included vertical space.

Toph wanted control of the brakes because they were metal.

I wanted to live.

We compromised.

Poorly.

On race morning, Cranefish Town was packed with spectators. The route wound from the market district, across the eastern bridge, around the old refinery, and down a long slope to the river square.

Competitors included messenger carts, sand-sailer adaptations, a pair of Fire Nation engineers with a pedal-driven machine, and one old woman pushing what appeared to be a wheelbarrow with absolute confidence.

Toph pointed toward her.

“She’s the threat.”

“You can tell?” I asked.

“She has no fear.”

Aang climbed into the front seat.

Katara sat beside him.

Toph and I took the rear.

“This is a date,” Aang announced.

“This is attempted murder,” Katara replied.

“Romantic murder.”

“Drive.”

The starting gong sounded.

Everything became noise.

Aang launched us forward with a burst of air.

I screamed.

Toph laughed.

Katara shouted, “LEFT!”

Aang shouted, “I KNOW!”

We turned right.

The Fire Nation pedal machine clipped a stack of hay bales. The wheelbarrow grandmother passed us on the inside.

Toph slapped both feet against the floor plate and bent the rear axle just enough to pivot us around a vegetable cart.

A cabbage rolled through the air.

Somewhere, I felt history repeat itself.

“We’re going too fast!” I yelled.

Aang looked over his shoulder.

“We’re in seventh!”

“That is not an answer!”

Katara bent a ribbon of water from the reservoir and froze it along one runner as we hit a patch of mud. The cart slid sideways, perfectly controlled for approximately two seconds and then absolutely not controlled at all.

Toph whooped.

I discovered new prayers.

We reached the eastern bridge in fourth place.

Aang could have won easily if he stopped pretending the machine mattered and simply airbent us down the route.

He refused.

“That’s cheating!”

“Bending propulsion is allowed!” Katara yelled.

“Too much is spiritually cheating!”

Toph shouted, “Your spirituality is losing!”

The bridge narrowed.

Two carts entered ahead of us side by side.

Aang pulled back.

I expected frustration.

Instead he laughed.

“We go over.”

Katara’s eyes widened. “Aang—”

Air hit beneath the cloth wing.

The cart lifted.

Not high.

High enough.

We sailed over the gap between the two competitors and landed with every wheel striking stone at once.

My teeth met hard enough to see stars.

Toph was laughing so violently she could barely bend.

Katara stared at Aang.

He grinned.

She grabbed his face and kissed him while he was still steering.

“We are going to die,” I said.

Toph slapped my knee. “Worth it!”

The refinery turn brought us beside the wheelbarrow grandmother.

She glanced over.

“Too many people!” she shouted.

“You’re terrifying!” Aang shouted back.

She smiled.

Then passed us again.

We finished third.

The grandmother won.

Nobody was surprised.

At the award table, Aang bowed to her.

“What’s your secret?”

She looked at him as if the Avatar were a somewhat slow child.

“Downhill.”

Toph nearly collapsed.

The prize money went to the city’s winter shelter fund. Our third-place ribbon went to Toph, who claimed she had contributed the most by preventing the rest of us from dying.

Katara argued that she had prevented at least two deaths personally.

I argued that I had served as ballast.

Aang argued that joy was its own contribution.

We threw snow at him.

That should have been the end of the day.

Instead, Aang dragged us to the festival proper.

We ate fried dough. Katara won a carved polar bear dog at a ring toss and insisted she had not used waterbending. Toph challenged a strength-test machine and broke it. I spent an irresponsible amount of money on roasted chestnuts.

For six hours, nobody asked Aang to mediate anything.

Nobody asked Katara to heal them.

Nobody asked Toph to build, teach, detect lies, or represent metalbenders.

Nobody handed me a form.

We were not symbols.

We were four idiots sharing one scarf because Aang had lost his, Toph refused to wear one properly, and Katara had decided hypothermia was a collective moral failure.

Near sunset, music began in the square.

Aang reached for my hand.

This time he did not scan the crowd first.

I noticed.

He noticed me noticing.

His fingers tightened.

“Dance?”

“I saw how you drove.”

“That’s unrelated.”

“It feels related.”

Katara took my other hand.

“Come on.”

Toph said, “I don’t dance.”

Three of us looked at her.

She sighed.

“I hate this family.”

“You chose us,” Aang said.

“Worst mistake of my life.”

She joined anyway.

Aang moved like air even with his boots on the ground.

Katara followed rhythm the way she followed water, graceful until she laughed too hard and missed a step.

Toph danced by feeling everyone else’s feet through the stone and then deliberately doing something different.

I was not good.

Nobody cared.

At one point Aang spun me beneath his arm, Katara caught me when I overbalanced, and Toph complained that our choreography was “aggressively sighted.”

So we changed it.

Toph put one hand on my shoulder, one on Katara’s. Aang kept contact through our linked arms. We stopped relying on visual cues and moved to pressure, rhythm, laughter, the vibration of drums under our feet.

Toph smiled.

Not because we had included her.

Because we had adapted together without turning adaptation into charity.

That distinction mattered.

Night settled over the square.

Lanterns reflected in patches of melted snow.

Aang pressed his forehead to mine when the music slowed.

“Terrible idea?”

I looked at Katara, cheeks pink from cold and dancing. Toph had stolen the third-place ribbon and tied it around her wrist like a championship belt.

“Terrible,” I said.

Aang smiled.

“Wonderful?”

I kissed him.

“Unfortunately.”

The terrible idea was an Air Nomad cultural center with a public kitchen, meditation hall, archive room, rooftop garden, and absolutely no clear source of funding.

Aang had drawn the first plan himself.

This was obvious because every corridor curved beautifully and none of the storage rooms were large enough to hold anything larger than a monk’s optimism.

Katara spread the papers over the table. “Where do supplies go?”

Aang pointed. “There.”

“That’s a window.”

“It could become shelves.”

Toph leaned over the plan, unable to see it and therefore judging it with complete confidence. “Floor’s bad.”

“You haven’t touched the floor. It doesn’t exist yet.”

“I can tell.”

I traced the public entrance. “If this is for teaching Air Nomad culture, who gets to teach?”

Aang’s excitement faltered.

That was the real question beneath all the architecture.

“I do, at first,” he said.

“And when people know parts you don’t?” Katara asked gently.

He looked at her.

There were scraps of Air Nomad history scattered across the world: temple records, old songs remembered imperfectly by families, artifacts in private collections, stories altered by a century of retelling. Aang carried more than anyone alive. He did not carry everything.

“I invite them,” he said slowly.

Toph tapped the table. “Even if they disagree with you?”

His mouth twisted.

“Especially then, probably.”

“That sounds awful.”

“It does.”

I smiled. “Still wonderful.”

Aang looked at the plans again, this time with less certainty and more possibility.

By midnight we had added storage, ramps, a community advisory table, a rule against treating every surviving artifact as sacred merely because it was old, and an entire page labeled THINGS AANG DOES NOT HAVE TO KNOW ALONE.

He circled that heading.

Then he drew a tiny sky bison beside it.

Toph felt the fresh ink with one fingertip.

“Terrible drawing,” she said.

“You can’t see it.”

“I can feel the lack of talent.”

Wonderful, unfortunately, survived another meeting.
